Empirical Research Plan: 1965 Head Start Roll-out, County “Poorest-300” Assignment

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (FRD) combined, where feasible, with Difference-in-Differences across cohorts.

Why FRD?  
• Treatment intensity—Head Start funding per poor preschooler and eventual child participation—jumps discretely at the poverty-rank cutoff that determined whether OEO sent grant-writing interns.  
• Counties could not manipulate their 1960 poverty ranking ex-post, and no other War-on-Poverty program used the same rule, delivering a quasi-experimental discontinuity that is plausibly exogenous.  
• Because not every “eligible” county ultimately received (or fully utilized) large Head Start grants, and some just-ineligible counties still obtained modest funding, the discontinuity is in the probability/intensity of treatment → fuzzy, not sharp, RD.  
• Outcomes (mortality of 5–9 y/o in the 1970s and adult schooling of 1990 Census/NELS cohorts) are observed well after the cutoff, so cohort comparisons over time help net out baseline differences—hence a supplementary DiD layer.

Econometrically:  
Stage 1:   HS_spending_{c} = α₀ + α₁·Above300_{c} + f(PovertyRank_{c}) + ε_{c}  
Stage 2:   Outcome_{c} = β₀ + β₁·Ť̂ HS_spending_{c} + g(PovertyRank_{c}) + υ_{c}

where f(·) and g(·) are local linear polynomials on either side of the cutoff.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Running variable: 1960 county poverty rank (1 = poorest).  
• Cutoff: Rank ≤ 300.  
• Treatment variable: Head Start intensity—e.g. 1968 Head Start federal outlays per poor 3-to-4-year-old (continuous).  

  – Binary alternative: Any Head Start grant by 1968 (dummy).

• Instrument: Indicator Above300_{c} (1 if rank ≤ 300).  
• Control group: Counties with poverty rank slightly worse than 300 (e.g. 301–600) inside a chosen bandwidth that did not receive intern assistance.  
• Treatment timing: Funding starts 1965–1966, peaks 1968–1972. Outcomes measured:

  – Health: 5–9 mortality rates 1973-1983 from immunizable/infectious causes.  
  – Education: Completed schooling among birth cohorts 1961-1968 (exposed) versus 1953-1960 (unexposed).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff: In absence of treatment, mortality/education trends would vary smoothly with poverty rank at 300.  
• Plausibility: 1960 poverty rank determined only this specific OEO help; no other discontinuous policy at the same threshold (per archival review).

A2. No sorting/manipulation of the running variable: Counties could not retro-actively change 1960 poverty rates or their rank.  
• Plausibility: Data compiled by Census before program conceived; manipulation impossible.

A3. Relevance: Above300 strongly predicts subsequent Head Start dollars/participation.  
• Plausibility: Historical spending data show 2–3× higher grants in eligible counties well into the 1970s.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Head Start activity in one county does not materially change outcomes in neighboring counties inside the bandwidth.  
• Plausibility: Preschool services are locally delivered; cross-county spillovers minimal, though we will test for spatial leakage.

A5. For FRD + DiD: Parallel pre-trends across cohorts on either side of cutoff.  
• Plausibility: We can test using pre-program child mortality 1950-64 and older cohorts’ schooling.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Other policies correlated with extreme poverty (e.g., Community Health Centers) could also jump at 300.  
  Mitigation: Assemble federal expenditure data for other War on Poverty programs; show no discontinuity at 300. Include these dollars as controls.

T2. Heterogeneous baseline demographic composition (race, urbanicity) could bias RD if non-linear.  
  Mitigation: Balance tests for 1960 covariates; include flexible controls; narrow bandwidth; employ bias-corrected RD (Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik).

T3. Mean reversion in mortality or schooling (poorer counties may have different trends).  
  Mitigation: Add DiD dimension—compare exposed (born 1961-68) vs. slightly older cohorts within county. A triple-difference design: (Above300 × ExposedCohort).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------- Load libraries -------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast felm/iv
library(rdrobust)    # RD inference
library(modelsummary)

# ------------- Load data ------------------
county <- read_csv("county_master.csv")   # one obs per county
# Key vars assumed in the CSV:
#  poverty_rank  : 1 = poorest
#  hs_pc68       : Head Start $ per poor 3-4 yo, 1968
#  mortality_73_83  : deaths per 100k age 5-9 from HS-amenable causes
#  schooling90      : avg years school 25-29 y/o, 1990 Census
#  pre_mortality50_60 : placebo outcome
#  other_fed_spend : Community Health Center $ etc.

# ------------- Generate running & treat ---
cutoff <- 300
county <- county %>%
  mutate(
    above300 = if_else(poverty_rank <= cutoff, 1, 0),
    running  = poverty_rank - cutoff   # centered running var
  )

# ------------- Main FRD (local IV) --------
# choose bandwidth with rdrobust
bw <- rdbwselect(y = county$hs_pc68, x = county$running)$bws[1,"h"]

# Local polynomial IV using fixest within ±bw
main_df <- county %>% filter(abs(running) <= bw)

iv_main <- feols(mortality_73_83 ~ 1 | hs_pc68 ~ above300 + running + I(running^2),
                 data = main_df, vcov = "HC1")

summary(iv_main)

# ------------- Robustness: covariate balance
cov_test <- feols(other_fed_spend ~ above300 + running + I(running^2),
                  data = main_df)
summary(cov_test)

# ------------- Placebo cutoff check -------
placebo <- feols(mortality_73_83 ~ above300_pl + running_pl + I(running_pl^2),
                 data = county %>% 
                   mutate(above300_pl = (poverty_rank <= 400),
                          running_pl   = poverty_rank - 400))
summary(placebo)

# ------------- Cohort DiD RD --------------
# assume long panel county_cohort with vars: exposed(=1 if birth 61-68),
# mortality_cohort, etc.

cc <- read_csv("county_cohort.csv")
cc <- cc %>% mutate(above300 = (poverty_rank <= cutoff),
                    running = poverty_rank - cutoff)

tri_diff <- feols(mortality_cohort ~ exposed * hs_pc68 | county + birth_cohort,
                  data = cc, cluster = ~county)

summary(tri_diff)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Direction: Negative effect on child mortality (i.e., lower deaths) and positive effect on completed schooling.  
• Magnitude priors:  
  – Mortality: 2–4 fewer deaths per 100,000 children aged 5–9 from immunizable causes—a 10–20 % decline vs. mean of ~15/100k.  
  – Education: +0.10 to +0.25 years of schooling (≈2–5 % of SD) for cohorts exposed in high-grant counties.

Effects likely similar in sign for black and white children, but baseline mortality higher for blacks implies larger absolute decline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Running variable not manipulable = 1  
C2. Covariates smooth at cutoff (to be shown) = 0.8  
C3. No other policy discontinuities = 0.8  
C4. Correct functional form / bandwidth choices = 0.7  
C5. Data density near cutoff adequate = 1  

Total (0–5): 4.3 → Strong but not perfect validity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
The above plan exploits the unique “poorest-300” rule as a quasi-experiment, delivering credible causal estimates of Head Start’s long-run health and educational benefits and permitting race-specific analysis in America’s poorest counties.
